source.title: Sockpuppetting: Jailbreaking LLMs Without Optimization Through Output Prefix Injection

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports jailbreak results using output prefills and optimized suffixes, but does not measure, remove, add, or rely on the claim’s difference-in-means refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The reported attack-success rates concern harmful-request compliance, but the attacks do not target or measure the single residual-stream direction. The paper’s discussion of acceptance sequences and model self-consistency is not a test of that direction. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper studies prefill and assistant-block suffix jailbreaks and reports only attack success rates. It never computes, ablates, adds or measures a refusal direction or any internal representation. It also does not cite the original single-direction paper. Its results bear on no version: V3 would need evidence that attacks suppress the direction, which is absent. The record's 'discusses' overstates the link, because the paper never discusses refusal directions. Its only mechanistic remarks concern self-consistency and refusal 'flipping', which are behavioural. Strictly, 'cites_only' is also inexact since the original is not cited; it is the closest enum value to 'neither tests nor uses'.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that small prefill ensembles make prefill attacks much stronger than the standard 'Sure, here is' prefill. They also conclude that rolling sockpuppetting beats their (low) universal GCG baseline, by up to 64 pp on Llama. An ablation equalizing the target sequence attributes much of that gain to acceptance-sequence design rather than placement, except on Qwen. They make no claim about refusal directions.
record.recipe_differences: No difference-in-means direction is identified or intervened on. The study uses output prefilling and gradient-optimized suffixes instead.
record.method_sensitivity: Prefill effectiveness varies by model and acceptance-sequence format. The paper also reports that equalizing the target sequence substantially shrinks the apparent placement advantage of sockpuppetting on Gemma and Llama, while Qwen retains a clearer lead.

fits_no_version.finding: Ensembles of trivial assistant-block prefills reach 22%, 90% and 99% ASR on Gemma-7B, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. Rolling assistant-block GCG reaches 31% (Gemma), 71% (Llama) and about 83% (Qwen) universal ASR. Part of the gain is due to the target-sequence choice.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Output-prefix injection elicits harmful compliance in open-weight instruct models, with effectiveness strongly dependent on prefix format and model.

fits_no_version.finding: Low no-attack compliance does not predict jailbreak robustness. Qwen refuses most without attack yet is most susceptible to prefills; Gemma often 'flips' back to refusal after the acceptance sequence.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Baseline refusal rate and robustness to prefill attacks are dissociable across models.

record.peer_reviewed: Published at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD) at ICML 2026
record.problems: Attack success is judged by a single Gemma-3-27B-it model, which the authors describe as lightly validated; manual inspection was qualitative rather than a quantified audit. Each attack is evaluated once per model and prompt using greedy sampling. The authors note that their GCG reimplementation uses different hyperparameters from the original and that its low baseline affects comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted from the claim-related findings recorded here. Results for unrelated attack baselines and figure-only values without a usable textual description were not extracted as exact rates.

untested.parts: Direction extraction, ablation, addition and capability retention: none performed.
No measurement of whether prefill or sockpuppet attacks suppress a refusal direction; no training against ablation.
No separation of harmfulness encoding from refusal.
No transfer of a direction across languages or models.
Qwen3-8B can reason, but thinking mode is not discussed and no direction is studied.

record.verdict_notes: Not a test of any version. The study is behavioural jailbreak work with a single lightly validated LLM judge and single greedy runs, and its GCG reproduction sits low relative to published values. Relation is downgraded from 'discusses' because the refusal-direction literature is never engaged.

versions.untested_parts: Direction construction, ablation, addition, refusal behavior after intervention, and retained capabilities.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed.
The attacks are not tested for suppressing the refusal direction, and no training against its ablation is evaluated.
No affine, cone, or multiple-direction account is tested.
No harmfulness judgment representation is separated from a refusal decision.
No cross-language or cross-model transfer of the direction is tested.
No refusal-training procedure or training stage is varied to test whether a removable direction forms.
No reasoning model is evaluated for the single-direction claim.

rows.subject: Gemma-7B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate harmful prompts without an attack
rows.value: over 93% refusal across all three models
rows.note: The text reports this as an aggregate across Gemma-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen3-8B; it does not give a separate exact rate for this model.
rows.check: Aggregate no-attack refusal rate (>93%) across all three models, attributed to Gemma-7B alone. The value is a baseline, not a result, and has no bearing on any version.
